title: Writing acceptance criteria
when: A plan needs the list of conditions QA will test, or the brief has goals but nothing a checker can say yes or no to.
prompt:
Goal: 3 to 7 criteria that each read as one observable fact about the files, which QA can mark pass or fail without guessing.
Steps:
1. Turn each thing the user asked for into a sentence that starts with a file or a screen: "index.html shows the opening hours for every day".
2. Make each criterion checkable by reading files or running a check: name the element, text, function or command.
3. Add one criterion for behavior when it matters: "submitting the empty form shows an error next to the email field".
4. Add the baseline the crew always needs: works at 375 px wide, no placeholder text, scripts parse.
5. Cut criteria that are taste (looks modern) or rewrite them as a fact (one accent color, body text 16 px or larger).
6. Keep 3 to 7; more than that means the job should be split.
Quality bar:
- Two different checkers would give the same verdict for each line.
- Each criterion maps to at least one task.
- No criterion asks for something the request did not imply.
Pitfalls:
- Criteria that restate the request ("a nice bakery site").
- Criteria about process (dev wrote tests) instead of results.
- Numbers with no source, such as "loads in 1 second", that nobody can measure here.
Verify:
- [ ] Each line names a file, element, command or output.
- [ ] Each line is pass or fail, never a score.
- [ ] Count is 3 to 7.
- [ ] Every user requirement appears.
Output: A criteria list as "- [ ] ..." lines, attached to the plan for QA.

examples.input: a todo app that saves my tasks
examples.output: - [ ] adding a task shows it in the list; - [ ] tasks survive a reload via localStorage; - [ ] app.js parses
